title: Effect of shot peening on fatigue strength of DED-Arc steel specimens with as-built surfaces
abstract: Abstract This screening study investigates the effect of shot peening and blast cleaning on the fatigue strength of additive manufactured steels structures by directed energy deposited-Arc (DED-Arc) with as-built surface condition. Specimens were manufactured from low-alloyed, low-alloyed high-strength, and austenitic stainless steel wire feedstock. Following specimen preparation surface peening was applied and specimens were characterized regarding surface topography, residual stress condition, hardness and microstructure. Fatigue tests were conducted with constant amplitude axial sinusoidal loading at a stress ratio of  R  = 0.1. The fatigue test results are further compared to specimens in as-built condition as well as milled DED-Arc specimens. It was found that shot peening led to fatigue strength improvement for all considered steel materials with the degree of improvement depending on the steel grade. Furthermore, the results indicate an influence from shot peening intensity on the increase in fatigue strength improvement, with lower peening intensity showing a less severe effect. The increase in fatigue strength due to shot peening can be linked to cold work hardening and the formation of compressive residual stress in the surface layer. Depending on the material, surface, and peening conditions, fatigue strength improvement of + 22–136% relative to the as-built condition could be determined after shot peening.

sections.heading: Introduction and state of the art
paragraphs: Additive manufacturing (AM) of metals is increasingly applied in industries, such as aviation, heavy equipment, tooling, mobility, construction and others. However, the processes establishing directed energy deposition (DED) are still more present in research projects rather than in engineering applications. Among these DED-processes, two main scenarios of usage are developing, first the advanced digitalized repair of complex large components or tools [ 1 ], and second, the additive manufacturing of original components intended to be integrated in a larger structure [ 2 ]. While the first scenario is rather familiar to conventional cladding and surfacing methods, the novelty of both scenarios is the complete digitalization of the entire process chain from design to post-processing. In both cases, lead time and secondary factors, such as delivery chains, multi-material use, functional grading, and beneficial carbon footprints, may prevail higher manufacturing costs compared to conventional manufacturing.

Products made by DED-processes are usually characterized by relatively large layer dimensions in the mm-range compared to those from powder bed processes. These layers are observable in heterogenous microstructures and coarse surface topographies with waviness up to, or even increasing, 1 mm. Additionally, the microstructure depends on the material behavior when melting, partial remelting, and multiple reheating is applied as a result from the deposition process. Accordingly, for most metallic materials made in the DED processes, a local heterogenous and anisotropic mechanical behavior must be expected. The surface waviness results in local stress concentration, and large geometric tolerances must be accepted. Resulting from this, DED components are usually machined to fulfill tolerance requirements, meet the requirements for non-destructive testing, ensure suitability for coating, and to avoid geometric stress concentrations, e.g., when fatigue loads are to be expected. However, different manufacturing scenarios yield feasibility limits for machining DED components. Examples are geometric constraints, when parts have narrow openings or cavities, or simply economical limits of entirely machining large and complex parts. No matter the reason, mechanical surface treatment may be an alternative solution to increase the surface resistance to fatigue crack generation. Among the different mechanical surface treatment methods, shot peening and blast cleaning are ideal to treat large, uneven surfaces with complex shapes.

sections.heading: DED-Arc of steel
paragraphs: DED-processes establish feedstock material in the form of filaments/wires or powder. The energy needed to melt material is provided by a laser, an electron beam, or an electric arc plasma [ 3 ]. This work focuses on the DED-Arc process according to ISO/ASTM 52900, also known as Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM), where wire feedstock is molten in an electric arc plasma. The process is derived from conventional gas metal arc fusion welding (GMAW) but serves in fully digitalized and automated process chains for additive manufacturing [ 4 ]. Exemplary uses of this process can be found manifold in the literature for titanium [ 5 ], aluminum [ 6 ], bronze [ 7 ], and steel [ 8 ,  9 ,  10 – 11 ].

In the past, most benefits of applying DED-processes were expected in the optimized material use and the limitations of material waste or scrap in the post-processing often referred to by an optimized by-to-fly ratio, e.g., for titanium alloys. Today, the focus has widened and the potential of AM for even rethinking the manufacturing of less vulnerable materials is investigated as well. The use of low-alloyed steel in DED-Arc may be counterintuitive at first sight due to the low cost of the material. However, DED-Arc with welding wire electrodes in the class of 350 to 900 MPa is a recent field of research aiming to provide large structural parts for demanding applications [ 2 ,  12 ,  13 ].

The focus of recent DED-Arc research is, next to less material-dependent process optimization, on predictive microstructure and material properties [ 10 ,  14 ,  15 – 16 ], residual stresses and distortion [ 17 ,  18 ,  19 – 20 ], buckling [ 21 ], and fatigue. The predictive design and manufacturing of complex parts is still challenging and one of the main issues in technology transfer to commercial markets.

Many process routes include some sort of post-building treatment to improve part properties. Post-processing of AM-made metals can be separated in mechanical, thermal, chemical and hybrid processes [ 22 ]. The thermal processes are applied to optimize microstructures and to reduce residual stresses. Mechanical processes include both surface peening and machining without and with material removal. The machining of wavy DED-surfaces reduces geometric notches significantly and hence yields higher fatigue strength. Investigating low-alloyed DED-Arc manufactured steel with milled surface, Karabulut et al. reported comparatively high fatigue strength corresponding to FAT 180 with a slope of  m  = 5 [ 23 ]. This was assessed to a fine grain microstructure paired with low porosity and low tensile residual stress. Braun et al. compared the fatigue properties of conventional and additive manufactured (DED-Arc, PBF-LB) AISI 316L [ 24 ]. It was found that textured columnar grains and tensile residual stress in DED-Arc lead to slightly lower fatigue performance compared to PBF-LB and as wrought material.

Regarding the influence of an as-built surface waviness on the resulting fatigue strength of DED-Arc material, Müller et al. [ 25 ] have shown that the fatigue strength may be improved by a factor of approximately 2 when DED-Arc surfaces are milled using high-strength low-alloyed steel (AM80). Similar trends were reported by Huang et al. [ 26 ] for structural steel ER70S-6, with the as-built surface causing a reduction in fatigue strength of approx. 35%, leading to a comparable fatigue performance to conventional S355 structural steel for milled surface condition and butt welds for the as-built surface respectively. Fatigue testing of DED-Arc high-alloyed steels AISI 308L and 316 L in milled and as-built surface condition also revealed a reduction in fatigue strength of approx. 40% due to earlier fatigue crack initiation caused by the as-built surface waviness [ 27 ,  28 ]. In [ 27 ] it was further reported that residual stresses as a result from electropolishing of specimens were found to negatively impact fatigue strength. Based on a limited test series and an evaluation using the effective notch stress concept, Bartsch et al. [ 29 ] numerically generated various surface waviness profiles through Monte Carlo simulations and investigated their influence on fatigue strength, indicating exponential decay of fatigue strength with increased surface waviness. However, the existing data on the fatigue behavior of DED-Arc material is still insufficient to experimentally validate the findings.

Investigations on DED-Arc aluminum materials further indicate a heightened detrimental effect of process-induced internal defects (e.g., pores, lack of fusion) on fatigue performance [ 30 ,  31 – 32 ]. Due to the higher susceptibility to pore formation during welding-based processing, such material imperfections are considered more critical for aluminum alloys.

In summary, prior research has identified characteristic microstructural features, process-related imperfections and residual stresses, as well as structural notches as critical factors influencing the fatigue behavior of DED-Arc components. However, the impact of commonly applied surface post-treatment methods, such as clean blasting or shot peening, has not yet been investigated in the context of DED-Arc manufacturing.

sections.heading: Fatigue strength improvement by shot peening
paragraphs: Shot peening is a well-proven and industrially established method to improve fatigue strength of unwelded components, such as springs, bearings, or gears [ 33 ,  34 ]. Compressive residual stress is generated near the surface, and the material is plastically deformed, causing cold work hardening. As a result, the fatigue strength increases, both the crack initiation life (effect of cold work hardening) as well as the crack propagation life (compressive residual stress).

Shot peening of welds is also effective for the enhancement of fatigue strength but is not represented in design standards, yet. Meta studies on shot peening of welds have proven that the improvement is mainly governed by stress concentration (resp. the weld detail) and the material grade [ 35 ,  36 – 37 ]. The peening parameters affect the depth of the compressive residual stress field and residual stress stability under cyclic loading. Peening intensity and the coverage should be controlled in order to ensure a robust compressive residual stress field [ 36 ]. Another limiting factor is yielding of the material in the close vicinity of the geometric notch, e.g., the weld toe. Butt welds with relatively mild notches show significant improvement of fatigue strength in the range of approximately 150–200% at 2 million load cycles. Sharp notches at fillet weld toes show less improvement and a strong effect from weld geometry and peening conditions [ 38 ,  39 ]. Hence, shot peening proves to be very effective to improve fatigue strength of welds if stress concentration is limited. This precondition may be fulfilled in DED-Arc specimens, but the positive effect needs proof.

In many potential industrial use cases, blast cleaning is used as post-processing of DED-Arc deposits to clean the surface and remove the oxygen layer or residues to further apply corrosion protection. This motivates to further quantify the fatigue performance of DED-Arc specimen in this condition. Accordingly, this study investigates effects of shot peening of DED-Arc steel specimens on their surface characteristics and the resulting fatigue strength. The fatigue strength is put in relation to unprocessed and machined surfaces.

sections.heading: Experimental
paragraphs:
The present study extends previous investigations on the influence of surface characteristics on fatigue strength for both machined and as-built surface conditions obtained for three different steel feedstock materials: a low-alloy steel S460–8MnSi7 (voestalpine Böhler 3Dprint AM46, hereafter AM46), a high-strength low-alloy steel S800–10NiMnMoCr8-7–6 (voestalpine Böhler 3Dprint AM80 HD, hereafter AM80), and a high-alloy austenitic stainless steel AISI 316L–X2CrNiMo17-12–2 (voestalpine Böhler 3Dprint AM316L, hereafter AM316L). The chemical compositions of the investigated feedstock materials are listed in Table  1 . This study further investigates the potential improvement in fatigue strength achieved by shot peening of the as-built surface. For the analysis of surface condition effects, thin-walled DED-Arc plates were manufactured, from which fatigue test specimens were mechanically extracted in building direction, and selected series were subsequently subjected to peening on all sides.

For specimen fabrication, a robot-guided DED-Arc setup consisting of a KUKA handling robot and a welding power source (Fronius iWave 400i AC/DC or TPS 400i) was employed. In all cases, a GMAW process with waveform-controlled dip transfer mode (cold metal transfer, CMT) was used. In accordance with previous investigations, thin-walled plates of approx. 350 × 230 mm were produced with alternating deposition direction each layer, using the experimental parameters shown in Table  2 .

Specimens for fatigue testing were subsequently extracted from the DED-Arc plates using water jet cutting and milling. The specimens were further split statistically to the different test series. Table  3  summarizes the test series considered in this study, including reference series originating from other studies. To ensure comparability with previous studies, the specimen geometries were selected accordingly, resulting in the use of different geometries for the respective test series. The applied specimen geometry for each test series is indicated in Table  3 , while detailed specimen dimensions are provided in Annex  1 .
 Table 3 Test series considered in this study AM46 AM80 AM316L Machined (from [ 40 ]) Specimen type I Machined (from [ 25 ]) Specimen type IV Machined (from [ 41 ]) Specimen type I As-built (from [ 40 ]) Specimen type I As-built Specimen type II As-built (from [ 41 ]) specimen type I As-built, shot peened (steel beads) Specimen type I As-built, shot peened (steel beads) Specimen type II As-built, shot peened (steel beads) Specimen type I - As-built, shot peened LI (glass beads) specimen type III - - AS-built, blast cleaned LI (corundum) Specimen type III -

To prevent crack initiation from geometric discontinuities at the specimen edges, the edges were chamfered and locally cold-worked after specimen segmentation. This included manual grinding of a chamfer based on the extent of surface waviness (approximately 1.0 × 45°) to reduce sharp transitions from waviness valleys at the edge transition as well as manual cold-working of the chamfer region using a carbide rod. Prior to testing, specimens with as-built and peened surface conditions were uniformly shot peened in accordance with industrial standards at OSK Kiefer GmbH (Germany). Shot peening was carried out manually using a round blasting agent (S230 steel beads, particle size 0.5–1.2 mm), an Almen intensity of 0.3–0.4 mmA, and a coverage of 1.5 × 98%. For AM80, the influence of shot peening parameters was additionally investigated. For this purpose, one specimen series was shot peened with glass beads at a reduced Almen intensity of 0.2–0.25 mmA at a coverage of 1.5 × 98% (shot peened (LI)). A further specimen series was blast cleaned using corundum EK24 blasting agent at low intensity without documentation of the Almen intensity (blast cleaned (LI)). As is common for blast cleaning, the target criterion was a visually uniform surface condition. Based on visual inspection and size comparison of blasting agent particle size with surface waviness profiles, it was determined that the shot sufficiently reached the bottom of the local notches. Figure  1  shows the final specimens in as-built and shot peened condition. Fig. 1 Visual representation of fatigue test specimen in as-built (top) and shot peened (bottom) condition used in this study; specimen dimensions given in Annex  1
The specimens were characterized with respect to surface characteristics and residual stress state; in addition, microstructure and hardness were analyzed, and fatigue tests were performed.

To analyze the nominal thickness and characterize the microstructure of DED-Arc components, metallographic cross-sections were prepared following the guidelines of ASTM E3-95 [ 43 ]. Initially, the samples were ground using SiC papers, polished with a 1 µm diamond suspension, and finally finished with colloidal silica (OPS). C-Mn steels were etched using 5% nitric acid, whereas austenitic stainless steel was etched using hydrochloric-nitric acid. Microstructural observations were conducted using optical microscopy (ZEISS Imager 2M2). Hardness measurements were carried out using the automated hardness testing system DuraScan 70. Hardness mappings with an indentation spacing of 0.1 mm were performed using HV0.05 or HV0.1 on smaller areas to gain insight into the spatial distribution of hardness in interlayer regions. These mappings were intended to identify localized zones of both hardening and softening within the specimens.

Residual stress measurements were performed using an XStress G2R X-ray diffractometer applying the sin 2 ψ method (cf. Figure  2 ). The applied measurement parameters are summarized in Table  4 . Nine measurement points at 5 mm spacing were evaluated along the gauge section on two representative specimens per series, extracted from different locations of the thin-walled plates. Residual stresses were determined in the loading direction, transverse to the deposition direction. In addition, residual stress depth profiles were obtained for specimens with peened surfaces, as illustrated in Fig.  2 . For this purpose, the surface was locally removed by electrolytic polishing in steps of approx. 20 µm, and the residual stress was determined incrementally. Prior to residual stress measurements, process residues and adherent slag were chemically removed by pickling using hydrochloric acid. Fig. 2 Residual stress measurement setup (left) and location of residual stress depth profile measurement (right) Table 4 XRD parameters used for surface residual stress measurements Exposure time: 5.0–8.0 s X-ray tube type: Cr (30 kV/9 mA) Numbers of tilt angles:  ± 5 Collimator: 3 mm Tilt angle:  ± 39°

Fatigue testing was performed using a universal resonance test machine (Type Sincotec SYSMOT, 100 kN) with force-controlled axial loading. The tests were conducted according to the pearl string method at a stress ratio of  R  = (σ min /σ max ) = 0.1 until complete specimen failure or the termination criterion of  N  = 5∙10 6  load cycles was reached. The data was further fitted to Basquin’s equation with best-fit slope according to DIN 50100:2022.

sections.heading: Surface topography, metallography, and hardness
paragraphs: To assess the as-built surface condition, multiple 2D measurement tracks with a measurement length of  l e  = 80 mm covering the gauge length were initially analyzed in terms of arithmetic mean waviness (Wa), maximum waviness height (Wz), and total waviness height (Wt). The results obtained from the individual measurement tracks are compared in Fig.  3 , with mean values and standard deviations reported in Table  5 . From the comparison, it is evident that the AM46 specimens generally exhibit lower waviness compared to AM80 and AM316L. Moreover, the lower scatter between individual measurement tracks indicates comparatively homogeneous surface characteristics. In contrast, measurements on AM80 and AM316L reveal higher deviations in surface topography, with mean total waviness heights of Wt > 1.0 mm and increased scatter between measurement tracks, indicating a more irregular statistical distribution of surface features, particularly for AM80. These differences are likely related to variations in melt viscosity and process dynamics, leading to local lateral layer displacements in the thin-walled structure. Notably, despite higher energy and material input, AM46 shows lower surface waviness than AM80. This observation contrasts with the findings reported in [ 44 ], where an increase in surface irregularities with increasing energy and material input was observed for constant material and system setup. Accordingly, influences related to material composition and system setup are assumed to play a significant role. Figure  4  (left) illustrates the macroscopic buildup geometry of specimens investigated in this study by means of binarized cross-sections. The results are consistent with the surface waviness measurements, revealing comparatively smooth surfaces for AM46, whereas AM80 and AM316L exhibit more pronounced surface irregularities. In direct comparison, AM80 is characterized by a higher number of sharp V-notches, whereas AM316L predominantly shows long-wavelength U-notches with flatter opening angles. A further comparison of the AM80 specimens investigated in this study with results reported in [ 13 ] reveals that, although manufacturing parameters were only modified slightly, severely different layer structures occurred. Specimens manufactured for this study in vertical 0° position showed relatively coarse surfaces with V-notches of approximately 110° similar to those of [ 13 ] manufactured in 75° horizontal position. Fig. 4 Exemplary binarized cross-sections used for determining nominal specimen thickness (left) and distribution of effective thickness used for fatigue testing (right)

Besides notch formation, the surface waviness led to a relatively large scatter in specimen thickness. The statistical distribution of the nominal specimen thickness is shown in Fig.  4  (right). Depending on the material and the applied process parameters, the mean thickness of the investigated test series ranges between 4.79 and 7.47 mm, with reduced wire feed rates generally resulting in thinner specimens. Furthermore, the statistical evaluation reveals increased thickness scatter along the build direction for specimens exhibiting higher surface waviness. Based on Eq. ( 1 ), effective nominal thicknesses of 6.26 mm (AM46), 4.24 mm (AM80), and 6.73 mm (AM316L) were derived and used for nominal stress evaluation in the fatigue tests (Fig.  5 ). Fig. 5 Micrographs of shot peened edge area for  a  AM46,  b  AM80, and  c  AM316L

As shown in Fig.  6 a–c, cross-section micrographs show ferritic-pearlitic microstructure for AM46, fine-grain-predominant bainitic microstructure with small fractions of martensite and retained austenite for AM80, and coarse-grained, epitaxial dendritic growth of austenite with δ-ferrite fractions for AM316L, which are in good agreement to previous published studies on DED-Arc processing using respective feedstock materials [ 14 ,  45 ,  46 ,  47 ,  48 – 49 ]. With focus on the effects of surface peening, all three investigated materials exhibit pronounced regions of plastically deformed microstructure in the near-surface region, extending to a depth of approx. 50 µm, indicating cold-work hardening of the surface layer. To further characterize the effective depth and impact of the surface treatment, additional hardness and residual stress measurements were conducted. Fig. 6 Hardness HV0.05 mapping of shot peened edge area for  a  AM46,  b  AM80, and  c  AM316L

The hardness mappings covering a region of 4 mm in build direction and 2 mm from the surface for shot peened and low-intensity peened specimens are shown in Figs.  6  and  7 , respectively. For AM46, the measurements indicate an average hardness of approx. 175 HV0.05, with a slight increase of roughly 15 HV0.05 in interlayer transition zones (cf. Figure  6 a). Pronounced surface hardening caused by shot peening is visible near the surface, with hardness values reaching up to 240 HV0.05. In contrast, hardness measurements for AM80 reveal variations of up to 50 HV between different layer zones (cf. Figures  6 b and  7 ). Reheated regions near layer interfaces show local softening that spatially coincides with geometric notches, which is consistent with previously reported results [ 25 ]. It should be noted that absolute hardness values differ by approximately 30 HV between Figs.  6 b and  7  due to the different test loads applied (HV0.1 and HV0.05) [ 50 ]. Only a minor hardness increase is observed near the shot-peened surface. This may be attributed to the limited strain-hardening capacity of the high-strength AM80 material, as indicated by the high yield-to-tensile strength ratio of approximately 0.8 reported in [ 14 ]. However, a localized hardness increase in the immediate surface layer cannot be excluded, as potential changes may remain below the minimum indentation spacing of 0.1 mm. The austenitic stainless steel AM316L exhibits comparatively homogeneous hardness values in the range of 195–210 HV0.05 without pronounced softening in the interlayer transition zones (cf. Figure  6 c), whereas significant surface hardening is observed in the near-surface region, with hardness values exceeding 400 HV0.05. Fig. 7 Hardness HV0.1 mapping of low intensity peened AM80 in notched regions

sections.heading: Residual stress condition
paragraphs:
The surface residual stresses were measured at 9 points on two representative specimens in as-built and peened condition for each test series. The results did not indicate significant changes in residual stress amongst different specimens and measurement location. The mean values and standard deviations are summarized in Table  6 . As-built specimens showed relatively low surface residual stress with magnitudes in the range of 14 ± 19 MPa to 26 ± 20 MPa, indicating a relaxation of process induced residual stress as a result of cutting the specimens. The surface residual stress after shot peening shows the introduction of pronounced compressive residual stress of − 271 MPa and − 333 MPa for AM46 and AM80, respectively. Compressive residual stress was found to be of lower magnitude at approx. − 100 MPa for shot peening (LI) and blast cleaning (LI) processes with reduced intensity. Additionally, the overall low standard deviation indicates a uniform peening process of the specimen surfaces.
 Table 6 Surface residual stress (mean and standard deviation from 2 × 9 measurement points along the gauge length of fatigue specimen) Surface transverse residual stress (MPa) AM46 AM80 AM316L As-built 26 ± 20 14 ± 19 n.a As-built, shot peened -271 ± 20 -333 ± 47 n.a As-built, shot peened (LI) - -108 ± 35 - As-built, blast cleaned (LI) - -103 ± 27 -

Figure  8  (left) shows the residual stress depth profiles additionally determined for AM46 and AM80 in different peening conditions. The residual stress depth profiles show distinct compressive residual stress fields depending on material and peening condition. Shot peening leads to compressive residual stress within approx. 500 µm from the surface for both AM46 and AM80, with slightly higher peak stress of − 500 MPa for AM80. In contrast, residual stress fields for shot peening (LI) and blast cleaning (LI) exhibit a reduced effective depth of approx. 250 µm from the surface as well as lower maximum residual stress for the blast-cleaned (LI) specimen. In addition, the cold work hardening can be concluded from the Full width at Half Maximum FWHM values (cf. Figure  8  (right)). Similar to the residual stresses, a pronounced broadening of the diffraction peaks is observed within 400–500 µm for shot peening and 200–250 µm for shot peening (LI) and blast cleaning (LI) from the surface, indicating an increased cold work hardening towards the surface. However, for AM316L no residual stress values could be assessed. The reason is the large grain size and the texture effect of the near-surface material. This requires a large measurement volume, see former investigations of Braun et al. [ 24 ]. Fig. 8 Residual stress depth profile (left) and FWHM (right) of shot peened and blast-cleaned DED-Arc specimens

sections.heading: Fatigue test results
paragraphs: Direct comparisons of the fatigue test results for specimens with machined, as-built, and as-built shot-peened surface conditions based on nominal stress evaluation are presented in Fig.  9 a–c for the respective materials, considering the effective specimen thickness determined from macrographs by statistical analysis of the width distribution (Method 2 according to [ 13 ]). The corresponding S–N parameters are listed in Table  7 . Fig. 9 Evaluation of the fatigue test data according to the nominal stress approach for  a  AM46,  b  AM80, and  c  AM316L Table 7 Fatigue data with Δσ calculated at  N  = 2∙10 6  load cycles Material Surface n  excl. run out) k Δσ 50%  (MPa) Δσ 95%  (MPa) T S,95/5 AM46 Machined 7 10.4 342 311 1.21 As-built 10 4.9 188 179 1.11 As-built (SP) 8 8.1 248 235 1.11 AM80 Machined 9 8.9 493 455 1.17 As-built 12 2.9 98 78 1.58 As-built (SP) 7 5.0 231 199 1.35 As-built (SP-LI) 16 5.1 191 124 2.39 As-built (BC-LI) 15 3.9 137 106 1.66 AM316L Machined 9 8.0 271 263 1.06 As-built 10 4.7 160 134 1.44 As-built (SP) 8 7.2 195 158 1.53

As expected, all investigated materials exhibit the highest fatigue strength in the machined surface condition. In this state, the S–N curves generally show comparatively shallow slopes, with increasing fatigue strength observed for materials of higher tensile strength.

In contrast, the as-built surface condition leads to a pronounced reduction in fatigue strength for all materials, accompanied by steeper S–N curves due to the notch effect of the surface waviness. This effect is most pronounced for the high-strength AM80 material, with a reduction from Δσ 50%  = 493 MPa in the machined surface condition to Δσ 50%  = 98 MPa in the as-built condition. Compared to the as-built fatigue data reported in [ 13 ], this represents a more pronounced reduction, which can be attributed to the incomparably high surface waviness described in Sect.  3.1 , leading to more severe notch effects. However, comparable fatigue strengths are reported in [ 51 ] for AM80 specimens with similar surface quality.

Shot peening of the as-built surface leads to an increase in fatigue strength for all investigated materials, which primarily results from a flattening of the S–N curve slope. Consequently, the beneficial effect of shot peening becomes particularly apparent in the high-cycle fatigue regime. For AM80, the influence of different shot peening parameters was additionally investigated. A lower fatigue strength improvement is observed for shot peening processes with reduced intensity. Shot peening with steel beads at higher intensity resulted in higher fatigue strength compared to shot peening at lower intensity and blast cleaning, which is consistent with the state of the art due to higher residual stress stability and more pronounced compressive residual stress fields beneath the surface [ 36 ].

Furthermore, it is noteworthy that for all test series of AM46 as well as for the machined, as-built, and as-built shot peened series of AM80, specimen failure occurred at  N  < 10 6  or the run-out criterion was reached, indicating an early knee point of the S–N curves. This aspect should be addressed in more detail in future investigations. However, for the comparative assessment of surface treatment effects, fatigue strengths at  N  = 2∙10 6  load cycles were considered in the present analysis.

Regarding the crack initiation sites observed in fatigue testing, optical examinations of specimens with mechanically machined surfaces (from [ 25 ,  40 ,  41 ]) revealed crack initiation originating from both the long and short specimen edges, with crack propagation perpendicular to the direction of the primary principal stress. For specimens in as-built and as-built (SP) conditions, crack initiation was identified at the valleys of the surface waviness profile due to notch effects and local cross-sectional reduction (see Fig.  10 ). A direct correlation between the crack initiation sites and the most critical regions of the surface profiles could not be established. As shown by detailed stress analyses for the AM316L specimens in the as-built condition in [ 41 ], crack initiation is assumed to be governed not only by maximum stress concentrations but also by statistical effects. In particular, for the AM46 specimen series, which exhibited a comparatively homogeneous distribution of surface waviness, several competing crack initiation sites were partly observed along the specimen surface within the gauge length. Where these cracks were located within a few layers, further crack growth resulted in ductile fracture of the bridging ligaments. This behavior was also observed for AM316L specimens at high stress ranges. Furthermore, two specimens of the AM316L as-built series showed simultaneous crack initiation from both specimen surfaces at the same position, resulting in comparatively low numbers of cycles to failure and an increased scatter range of the S–N curve (cf. Fig.  9 c). Fig. 10 Location of crack initiation for representative specimens in as-built and as-built (SP) condition

For a direct comparison of the effects of the as-built surface condition and subsequent surface peening on fatigue performance, Fig.  11  compares the fatigue strengths for Δσ evaluated at 2·10 6  load cycles. Fig. 11 Comparison of fatigue strength with reference to Δσ calculated at 2·10 6  load cycles depending on surface condition

For AM46, the as-built surface condition results in a reduction in fatigue strength of approximately − 45% relative to the machined surface condition, while shot peening leads to an increase in fatigue strength of about + 32% compared to the as-built condition. Overall, the investigated test series exhibit a comparatively low scatter, which can be attributed to the uniform as-built surface quality characterized by low surface waviness.

The high-strength AM80 material shows a pronounced sensitivity to the notch effect of the as-built surface, with a fatigue strength reduction of approximately − 80% compared to the machined surface condition. It should be noted that the surface waviness resulting from the present process parameters is comparatively high relative to the investigations reported in [ 13 ], leading to a correspondingly higher reduction in fatigue strength. Compared to the as-built state, surface treatment results in fatigue strength increases of + 40% for blast cleaning (LI), + 95% for shot peening (LI), and + 136% for shot peening at higher intensity. This trend correlates with the more pronounced compressive residual stress fields observed in the residual stress measurements at higher peening intensities. In addition, an increased scatter of the S–N curves is evident particularly for the blast cleaning (LI) and shot peening (LI) series. This is presumably related to an influence of specimen geometry, as these series were tested using a reduced specimen width (specimen type III), which likely insufficiently captures the statistical distribution of surface waviness features. Accordingly, the specimen width was adapted for the subsequent test series (specimen type II), resulting in comparatively lower scatter. The interaction between surface characteristics, specimen design, and their influence on fatigue test results should therefore be addressed in future investigations to enable recommendations for consistent testing conditions.

For the austenitic stainless steel AM316L, the as-built surface condition leads to a fatigue strength reduction of −41% compared to the machined surface condition. Despite the significantly higher surface waviness, the resulting reduction in fatigue strength remains at a level comparable to that of AM46, which is likely to be attributed to the higher toughness of AM316L. Shot peening increases the fatigue strength by approximately + 22% relative to the as-built condition. The comparatively lower improvement in fatigue strength compared to the investigated carbon steels may be associated with nonlinear cyclic hardening behavior and a tendency towards cyclic softening as shown by Zhou et. al. [ 52 ] in the LCF regime but should be assessed in the scope of further research.

sections.heading: Conclusions and outlook
paragraphs: This initial experimental screening study investigated the fatigue strength of as-built, shot peened, and blast cleaned specimens manufactured by the DED-Arc process from low-alloy, high-strength low-alloy, and austenitic stainless steel feedstock materials. The specimens were prepared in accordance with previously published studies and comparatively characterized with respect to surface characteristics, metallography, residual stresses, and fatigue performance. The main findings of the study can be summarized as follows: Depending on feedstock material and manufacturing conditions, the surfaces of thin-walled DED-Arc structures exhibit significant differences in height, geometric shape, and statistical distribution of surface waviness, and consequently in the distribution of the nominal cross-section. Although the manufacturing parameters of AM80 were comparable to those used in a previous study, a change in the DED-Arc setup resulted in increased surface waviness, highlighting the influence of the specific DED-Arc setup on surface quality. Surface peening induced cold-work hardening and compressive residual stress fields, with magnitude and penetration depth depending on peening intensity and material. Shot peening with steel beads and higher Almen intensity resulted in more pronounced compressive residual stress fields compared to shot peening with reduced Almen intensity and blast cleaning. Independent of the investigated material system, a reduction in fatigue strength due to the notch effect of the as-built surface condition was observed, with the high-strength low-alloy steel exhibiting the most pronounced fatigue strength reduction. Surface shot peening led to an increase in fatigue strength for all investigated materials compared to the untreated as-built condition, ranging from + 22% for the austenitic stainless steel to + 136% for the high-strength low-alloy steel. In agreement with the residual stress measurements, lower peening intensities resulted in a reduced fatigue strength improvement.

Overall, this screening study demonstrates the general potential of surface peening to enhance the fatigue performance of DED-Arc steel components with unmilled as-built surfaces. As DED-Arc components or thin-walled specimens are frequently subjected to surface blasting for optical or functional reasons after manufacturing, potential surface post-treatments and their influence on fatigue performance should be carefully considered in fatigue testing.

Building on the present results, further investigations should aim to quantitatively assess the fatigue strength improvement and the underlying mechanisms, particularly with respect to material dependency as well as the magnitude and morphology of surface waviness. It is expected that the fatigue strength enhancement depends on the severity of surface waviness and the associated notch effect. Accordingly, systematic variation of surface characteristics, for example through process parameter modification, combined with an evaluation based on stress concentration factors and the effective notch stress approach, is expected to provide further valuable insights.

Furthermore, the increased scatter observed in fatigue tests using specimens with reduced width in the highly stressed cross-section area indicates an insufficient representation of the statistical distribution of surface waviness features. This highlights the need to carefully consider surface quality in specimen design, which should be addressed in more detail as a scope of further research.
